cells.tense: You're keeping two things alive at once, and neither one is slipping.
cells.ask: Offer one finished thing to someone who can tell you they saw it — let being witnessed be the completion, and notice what loosens when it lands.
cells.core:
You're carrying two needs and giving each its due. Nobody's dropping, nothing's forced, and the care itself is what keeps the whole thing standing. You know how much is enough, and you stop there, which is rarer than pushing through. The demands don't harden you and the softness doesn't scatter you. You keep the people near you in view while you hold the weight, and that takes more than either one alone.

A kitchen where the bread is out of the oven and the table is set — that's what steady looks like here. You bring something all the way through and then you hand it off. Finishing isn't loss; it's what the work was for. Let someone say what it took, and let that be the last step rather than a vanity you skip.
cells.sheetLine: You tend it well and you know when it's done.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with patient, responsible care
cells.place: the threshold where something is finished and ready to be let go

cells.tense: You're already past this ending, planning the next thing before the current one has landed.
cells.ask: Let one thing finish before you imagine what comes after it — stay with what's done until it's actually done, and let the dreaming come from what's been lived through rather than what you're bracing against.
cells.core:
You're tending ahead of the thing you're tending. The next version, the next step, the next opening — you're already there, holding both the current work and everything it might become. The caring is real. But nothing gets to arrive before you've already moved on, so what you're holding never feels finished and the holding starts to wear at you.

When it's well, the care doesn't exhaust. You hold what's growing without clutching it, and things move at their own pace because you're not pushing. A garden bed where the seedlings come up in their own time, not because you pulled them — that's what trusting it looks like. What you imagine is meant to flow from what you've actually been through. Let one thing land before you pick up the next.

cells.tense: You set this down and part of you is still standing where it was, as if it could be picked up again.
cells.ask: Keep hoping for one thing you've stopped tending — not by pushing effort at it, but by letting yourself want it again somewhere with no weight on it, and watch whether the wanting starts to move.
cells.core:
There's something you finished, or nearly finished, and you stepped away. The tending stopped. Not because the thing was wrong — something in you left the room before the work was done, and you can still see it from where you stand. The care didn't disappear; it just quit moving.

A garden where the beds are turned and the last row is planted — that's what steady looks like here. Care doesn't exhaust there. You hold space for what's growing without clutching it, and things reach their end because you stayed long enough to see them through. What's missing isn't effort. It's the willingness to shine a light on what you already built, and to be glad when it's finished.
cells.sheetLine: You left the work before it was finished, and you're still standing near it.

cells.tense: The tending is happening — you're still doing it — but you're talking as if the hands aren't yours.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been chalking up to timing or luck or someone else's doing, and say out loud that you're the one who's been tending it — not as a confession, as a receipt.
cells.core:
You've been the one keeping this alive. The steady attention, the carrying, the choice to keep showing up — it's yours, and you've been describing it as just what happened. The care keeps running. Saying so hasn't started. The work is real and the credit for it is sitting unclaimed.

A workbench where a project sits half-finished, tools still where you left them — that's what honest looks like here. You bring something to its end and then you set it down, and being seen doing it is not a defeat; it's what the tending was for. Tell one person what you've actually been carrying. Put your name on it.
cells.sheetLine: You've been the one tending this, and you've been saying it happened on its own.
